generatedCommentsNodes.comment: Test-fixture drift: The centroid coordinates shift in the 5th–6th significant digit (e.g. `-0.030548102…` → `-0.030548143…`). This is expected because removing the no-op conversion changes the internal computation path (fewer intermediate objects, potentially different summation order in the centroid aggregate). Worth a brief note in the PR description so reviewers don't mistake it for a regression.

The core rule in `ReplaceTypeConvertingEvalWithAliasingEval` is well-structured: it correctly guards on `FieldAttribute` (not `ReferenceAttribute`) and on data-type equality before eliding the conversion, and it is placed before `ReplaceAliasingEvalWithProject` so the aliasing-eval → project pipeline can collapse the now-trivial `Eval` into a `FieldAttribute` reference. The merged physical-plan test in `#0E2GN` is a solid improvement over the previous two separate tests, and it resolves the prior `TODO` by asserting `useDocValues == true` for the `to_geopoint` variant.

Rule scope is `Eval`-only: The rule extends `OptimizerRule<Eval>`, so it only fires when the convert function sits inside an `Eval` node. In the `stats centroid = st_centroid_agg(to_geopoint(location))` case this works because the planner materialises the conversion as a separate `Eval` below the `Aggregate` (visible in the old nested test's pre-optimisation plan). If a future planner change inlines the conversion directly into the aggregate expression (bypassing an `Eval`), this rule would silently stop applying. A brief comment on the rule noting this dependency on the planner emitting an `Eval` for the conversion would help future maintainers.

Hmm, why only in case of field attrs? Wouldn't this more general optimization also work?
```suggestion
                if (fa.dataType() == convert.dataType()) {
```

I only changed FieldAttribute because my primary goal was to enable lucene optimizations done by physical planning, and ReferenceAttributes that hide FieldAttributes were the main issue. Expanding to a wider scope could make sense, but also does not change performance in any way at all. The current PR makes one query 75x faster! I was already mildly concerned that my changes would have some subtle unforeseen side-effects, so did not want to widen the scope beyond what I actually needed.
